extracted.intended_audience: media scholars, journalism students, and newsroom practitioners (editors/reporters)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and organizational practices that determine which occurrences are identified, assigned, and placed as news in newspapers and television newscasts — emphasizing territoriality, specialization, editorial negotiation, and resource allocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for staff reporters over stringers
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors prefer stories by salaried reporters to those by stringers; staff work is favored even when supplied material is superior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasons include the organization’s financial investment in salaried reporters and the legitimating function of employing staff. Examples: photography editors rarely accept stringers' shots and will print a staff member’s picture 'even if the wire-service’s picture was photographically superior.' Stringers are used mainly in dire need (e.g., unexpected midnight riots) and avoided when coverage can be planned.

rubrics_metrics.name: News net is hierarchical; reporter status matters
rubrics_metrics.description: The news net is a hierarchical system of information gatherers, and the status of reporters in the news net may determine whose information is identified as news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Higher-status reporters (salaried, bureau staff) and those attached to legitimized beats are more likely to have their copy used and placed prominently. Example: bureau chiefs asserting 'I have nine reporters down here' to claim stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional centrality / legitimacy of sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories generated at centralized, legitimated institutions (beats and bureaus) are favored over occurrences at uncovered locations or grassroots events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reinforces the legitimacy of institutions hosting beats and privileges occurrences tied to recognized organizations. Anti-pattern: ignoring issue-oriented debates among working-class or unassigned social movement actors because they lack institutional hosting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumptions about readers’ interests
rubrics_metrics.description: News net incorporates three assumptions about readers’ interests: (1) Readers are interested in occurrences at specific localities. (2) They are concerned with the activities of specific organizations. (3) They are interested in specific topics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These assumptions shape reporter dispersion (geographic nets, organizational beats, topical departments). The author notes geographic territoriality as the most important of the three methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic territoriality (territorial responsibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: News organizations divide the world into areas of territorial responsibility; these divisions replicate the organization’s notion of its news mission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Territorial desks (metropolitan, national, foreign) and bureau claims are determined by proximity and organizational mission. Physical proximity often determines assignment (e.g., City Hall reporters get nearby dull hearings). Disputes over classification (local vs national) can affect placement and which anchor reads a story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational specialization: beats and bureaus
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish beats and bureaus at organizations associated with the generation of news and holding centralized information (e.g., UN, City Hall, police).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters may be based at the organization's building or tracked from city room desks; supervision and reporting chains reflect bureaucratic structures (bureau chiefs, metropolitan editor). Beats structure routinized access to sources and determine who 'owns' stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topical specialization (independent topical departments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Topical departments (finance, sports, family/style, culture, education) are independent with their own budgets and editors who may bypass territorial desks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Topical editors are told how many columns/pages to fill, may select their own pictures and display, and report directly to managing/executive editors. Despite independence, topical specialists are subordinate in practice to territorial editors and rarely push for front-page items frequently (e.g., family/style offers rarely).

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of territoriality over topical specialization
rubrics_metrics.description: Territoriality often takes precedence over topical specialization when claims overlap.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In conflicts (e.g., a sporting event tied to a place vs education), a territorial desk with physical proximity is more likely to be assigned routine coverage. Examples show bureaus negotiating and foisting dull hearings onto others based on availability and proximity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial negotiation and competition for assignments
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters and editors compete and negotiate for assignments and placement; editors act as representatives of 'self-interested fiefdoms' yet share the purpose of producing news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assignments and story placement are accomplished through bargaining at desk-level and managerial conferences; personal and inter-departmental jockeying affects which occurrences are identified as news. Friendly but fierce competition shapes outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of managing/executive editor as coordinator
rubrics_metrics.description: The managing/executive editor coordinates territorial and topical editors, revises plans as the day progresses, and heads negotiations about which items are truly important news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordination mitigates desk-level informational blind spots (e.g., national editor unaware of local breaking news). The managing editor uses tools like wire and desk budgets and evening meetings with assistants to shape page plans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of wire-service and desk budgets to allocate resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Wire services and desk editors transmit daily 'budgets' specifying story slugs, one-sentence elaborations, and expected lengths; budgets act as resource-allocation plans for column inches or air time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Budgets help editors and managing editors assess flow of occurrences and decide which stories to develop for page one or telecast. Television budgets specify feet of film; newspaper budgets specify 'takes' (pages of copy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Daily editorial conference determines front-page allocation
rubrics_metrics.description: A daily editorial conference (executive/managing editor plus territorial and topical editors) collectively assesses stories and codes which items are important for front-page placement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each editor arrives with items their reporters will file; executive asks 'What have you got?' and editors argue/offer stories. Decisions emerge from group negotiation and mutual boundaries rather than absolute objective standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance among desks as an editorial objective
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors seek some balance among international, national, and metropolitan desks on page one (Sigal's 'ideal balance'), and monitor deviations from that balance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sigal's balance variation index (difference between actual and ideal distribution) is used as an empirical measure; newsrooms tend toward a loose or ideal balance through ongoing negotiation. Overrepresentation of national stories can reflect resource distribution (more national reporters).

rubrics_metrics.name: Boundaries of front-page suitability (peer norms)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are mutually determined boundaries about what items may be offered for page one; colleagues will judge poor suggestions harshly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peer ridicule (e.g., proposing a small fire or routine college game for page one) enforces professional norms and constrains what editors offer; topical editors rarely propose front-page items to avoid stepping outside boundaries unless the item is exceptional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexibility vs rigid delineation in assignment rules
rubrics_metrics.description: News organizations maintain formal rules but require flexibility; rigid delineations can impede acting on unanticipated situations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Times rule that any reporter sent outside U.S. reports to international desk, but the traveling reporter may file for multiple desks. Negotiated flexibility is organizationally necessary to handle unforeseen events and overlapping interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slug selection as essence-of-story coding
rubrics_metrics.description: A story’s 'slug' (one-word label plus brief elaboration) encapsulates its essence and is attached to all materials for that story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choosing the slug involves deciding the essence of the story; ongoing stories receive consistent slugs day-to-day. Slugs assist in budgets and editorial coordination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical visibility and desk placement affect assignment likelihood
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters jockey for desks from which they can be noticed; physical placement in the newsroom affects whether editors assign them stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Partitioned offices for topical specialists reduce visibility; hidden desks (e.g., behind a support column) may lead to reporters being overlooked. Desk location thus functions as an informal selection lever.

rubrics_metrics.name: Display and layout influence story placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Topical editors may determine picture selection and 'display' (layout) for their departments, and assistant managing editors expect departments to fill specified columns/pages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a story is rejected for page one, an editor may be told to 'do a good display' on the department page (e.g., page three). Space allotments influence whether an item is pursued for front-page vs departmental display.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsworthiness assessed by potential audience affected ('number of persons affected')
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors often weigh the number of persons an occurrence would potentially affect when assessing importance, significance, and interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under this supposition, international stories (affecting many) tend to appear more often front-page than national or metropolitan stories; this heuristic informs negotiation and desk priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection reproduces social hierarchies and biases
rubrics_metrics.description: Patterns of news selection (e.g., privileging events involving suburban whites over urban blacks) reinforce social positions and institutional legitimacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The routine deeming of some events as 'not news' (small fires, petty crimes) institutionalizes value judgments about whose lives and occurrences matter; editors' choices reproduce societal inequalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification disputes (local vs national) shape handling
rubrics_metrics.description: How an item is coded (local vs national) carries consequences for placement, which anchor reads it, and which desk handles it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classification is negotiated; examples include dispute over Henry Cabot Lodge's arrival being coded as national lead versus local item. Coding thus is a strategic editorial decision affecting prominence.
